intro: Section 32.3 covers late adulthood: its developmental tasks (Table 32-18), the demographics of the aging population (Tables 32-19 and 32-20) and longevity, the biologic changes of aging by system (Table 32-21), life expectancy (Table 32-22) by sex, race and region, the effects of exercise and diet (Table 32-23), stage theories of late life from Freud, Erikson, Kohut, Neugarten and Levinson (Table 32-24), the stability of personality, and the psychosocial aspects of aging: social activity, ageism, chronic conditions (Table 32-25), transference and countertransference, socioeconomics, retirement, sexual activity and long-term care. US figures are as the book gives them. Update boxes add current Census and NCHS figures, a correction to the book's 2013 life expectancy, the WHO Global report on ageism, what Medicare covers today (mental health, prevention and nursing homes), and US and Philippine retirement and senior-citizen benefits.
objectives: Describe the developmental tasks of late adulthood and the main demographic trends of the older population, including the oldest-old.
Distinguish normal biologic changes of aging by organ system from disease.
Interpret life-expectancy data by sex and race, and explain the health effects of exercise and diet in old age.
Compare the stage theories of late life (Erikson's integrity versus despair and others in Table 32-24) and what is known about personality stability.
Recognize ageism, transference and countertransference with older patients, and the psychosocial issues of retirement, sexuality and long-term care.
